top3.why: A spokesperson for the anonymous collective behind Luigi Mangione's legal fund presents "Depose," a book arguing his case is really about the right to health care in America. Wooden Shoe is the natural room for this — anarchist bookstore meets explicitly political publishing (Ill Will Editions, distributed by MIT Press), out the next day. Free, South Street, easy walk from Point Breeze.

Bob Mould's Sugar reunite to play Copper Blue, the 1992 NME Album of the Year that bridged Hüsker Dü's hardcore roots into melodic alt-rock — essential listening for anyone who traces post-hardcore's lineage. A genuinely rare reunion show at a venue built for it. Tuesday's second Philly night, same tour, is a fallback if this one's sold out by the time you look.

The closing night of HOMEPLACE screens a film by Walé Oyéjidé — an award-winning fashion designer turned filmmaker — followed by a conversation with Àrokò Cooperative's design director. Small sliding-scale art space on Pine Street, Center City; the kind of one-off programming that doesn't repeat.

top3.why: The "Professors of Urgh" (Chaki and Chris Slusarenko) bring their touring presentation of URGH! A MUSIC WAR, the 1981 concert film that's basically a time capsule of punk and new wave's first wave — Devo, the Dead Kennedys, Gang of Four, Klaus Nomi. PhilaMOCA is exactly the room for it. Doors 7:00 PM, screening 7:30 PM, $17.

Alysia Li Ying Sawchyn and Meghana Mysore co-launch their new books — I Have This Thing for Flowers and Let All Our Ghosts Depart — at the Head & the Hand, a scrappy independent press and bookstore in Fishtown. Twin debuts, built-in conversation between the two writers. Fishtown, roughly near the Berks stop on the Market-Frankford Line (noting that from general knowledge of the corridor, not the listing itself).

Taylor Kelly — a Philly-scene fixture with a voice rooted in jazz, soul, and funk — plays an intimate early set at 48 Record Bar before the club spins a classic LP start to finish for a listening session. This is exactly the small-room, record-store-adjacent night that's easy to miss. Old City, a few blocks from the 2nd St stop on the Market-Frankford Line.

top3.why: Jaz Brisack, the Rhodes Scholar-turned-barista who co-founded Starbucks Workers United, talks through "Get on the Job and Organize" — a practical account of beating union-busting from the inside. Timely labor organizing at the bookstore built for it. Free, South Street.

Free, open-air "Creative Music" — the free-jazz/AACM-adjacent tradition Philly claims through Coltrane and Sun Ra — performed in Christ Church's gardens as part of the Collective Futures series. Polymodal improvisation outdoors, no ticket required.

Three Latina horror authors — Ann Dávila Cardinal and Diana Rodríguez Wallach among them — read and discuss short horror fiction for Latine Heritage Month at Taller Puertorriqueño, North Philly's long-running Latino cultural arts center. A genuinely specific intersection of horror and literature you won't find on a bigger stage. Norris Square, North Philly; nearest Market-Frankford El stop is roughly Somerset or Huntingdon, about a half-mile off (going by the area's general layout, not a stated transit line).

top3.why: The Thomas Edison Film Festival and The Rotunda team up for three short films plus a Q&A and a live jazz set from Black Buttafly — film, music, and community activism in one free night. Exactly the kind of one-off, multi-disciplinary programming The Rotunda does best outside its two standing weeklies. University City, on the Rotunda's usual turf.

The Dillinger Escape Plan — the band that basically defined mathcore/metalcore chaos in the 2000s and has only sporadically reunited since disbanding — play Underground Arts as part of Philly Music Fest. A genuinely rare chance to see them; this isn't a tour that happens often.

A community town hall in North Philadelphia with State Rep. Malcolm Kenyatta — a direct line to an elected official on what's happening in the neighborhood and what can be done at the state level. Free, with food and kids' activities. (The listing doesn't give a specific street address — confirm the exact location before heading out; North Philadelphia isn't walkable from Point Breeze, so plan transit once you have it.)

top3.why: Philly punk institution The Dead Milkmen ("Punk Rock Girl," "Bitchin' Camaro") play a general-admission show at Laurel Hill Cemetery — about as atmospheric a room as October offers. Local legends in a genuinely unusual venue. East Falls; reachable by bus along Ridge Avenue or Regional Rail to Allegheny (general knowledge of the area, not confirmed against a transit line in the listing).

Chicago's Deadly Prey Gallery sets up a month-long all-horror poster exhibition at PhilaMOCA, with founder Brian Chankin on hand Friday selling prints before introducing a screening of Dario Argento's PHENOMENA (1985) — the giallo master at his strangest (Jennifer Connelly, telepathic bond with insects, a chimpanzee with a razor). Gallery's open 5–9 PM, free; the screening is $10 at 9 PM.

The Soapbox — a community print shop and zine library — throws its goodbye party on its last day at this Kingsessing location. A one-time chance to see this DIY print/zine space before it's gone from here. Southwest Philly; likely reachable by bus along Woodland or Chester Ave (general sense of the area, not a confirmed route).

top3.why: Wooden Shoe Books turns 50 and marks it with a block party on South Street — half a century as Philadelphia's anarchist bookstore and a genuine anchor of the city's radical politics. This is a milestone, not a standing weekly: it won't come around again. Free, South Street, easy walk from Point Breeze.

Philadelphia-born artist Peggy Reavey — who met David Lynch at PAFA, married him, and played a real creative role in his early films — introduces screenings of his 1969 and 1970 shorts THE ALPHABET and THE GRANDMOTHER, both shot in their Fairmount home. A rare chance to hear Lynch's formative work discussed by someone who was actually there.

Ratas En Zelo headline a queer/Latinx metal-punk bill with Myles of Destruction, Depresión Tropical, and Night Fury at The Rotunda — exactly the kind of multi-interest, easy-to-miss DIY show this venue does best outside its two standing weeklies.

top3.why: Algernon Cadwallader — the Philly band whose name is basically shorthand for the 2000s emo revival — play a just-announced memorial show for a late friend, with all proceeds going to Savage Sisters' harm-reduction work. Genuinely rare: this isn't a standing tour, it's a one-off benefit. It's in Bensalem (Bucks County), about 15 miles from Center City — worth the trip for this bill specifically.

Acid Mothers Temple — the long-running Japanese psychedelic/noise collective that's basically a rite of passage for anyone into heavy, droning, improvised rock — play MilkBoy. A genuinely rare U.S. stop for a band whose live shows are the stuff of noise-rock legend.

A guided immersive theatrical walk through Elfreth's Alley, meeting six real past residents — portrayed by local actors — spanning 260 years of working-class life on America's oldest continuously inhabited residential street. Revives the alley's own street-theater tradition from the 1930s–40s. Old City, $15.
